title: Kepler-90i: a deep convolutional neural network finds an eighth planet in archival Kepler data
summary: A Google/UT Austin neural network found Kepler-90i in archival Kepler data; NASA announced it on 14 Dec 2017 and the AJ published it on 30 Jan 2018.
account: On 14 December 2017 NASA announced that a deep convolutional neural network built by Christopher Shallue (Google Brain) and Andrew Vanderburg (University of Texas at Austin, NASA Sagan Fellow) had identified an eighth planet, Kepler-90i, in archival data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The network was trained on about 15,000 previously vetted Kepler signals, correctly identified true planets and false positives 96 percent of the time in testing, and was then applied to 670 known multi-planet systems to search for weak transit signals missed by earlier methods. Kepler-90i, a rocky planet about 30 percent larger than Earth with a 14.4-day orbit, was statistically validated together with Kepler-80g, an Earth-sized sixth planet in a resonant chain. The peer-reviewed paper appeared in the Astronomical Journal on 30 January 2018.
purpose: Built to classify Kepler transit signals as planets or false positives and to recover planets missed by earlier searches; this benefit was that purpose.
system: Deep convolutional neural network for Kepler transit-signal classification (Shallue and Vanderburg)
developer: Google (Christopher Shallue, Google Brain) with Andrew Vanderburg (University of Texas at Austin)
deployer: Shallue and Vanderburg, applied to NASA Kepler archival data

ratings.reason: NASA's Paul Hertz said that discoveries were lurking in archived Kepler data awaiting the right tool; the archive yielded two newly validated planets without new telescope observations by the authors, whose validation used Kepler data and follow-up observations that other observers had already uploaded to the Kepler Community Follow-up Program.

Astronomy gained a validated eighth planet and the first exoplanetary system known to have eight planets, tying the Solar System; this is a knowledge gain for a specialist community rather than a population-level benefit.

ai_role.statement: The neural network ranked the weak Kepler-90i transit signal above false positives in systems that earlier automated and human searches had already examined; the authors then statistically validated both new planets. The AI did the identification; validation used conventional methods.

must_hold: The host star's light curve must contain the transit at detectable but sub-threshold signal-to-noise
Validation must rule out astrophysical false positives independently of the classifier

echoes.setting: AstroNet-K2 applied to K2 mission data; two previously unknown super-Earths identified and validated (Dattilo, Vanderburg, Shallue et al., accepted to AJ)

headline: Google neural network finds an eighth planet, Kepler-90i
metric: a rocky planet about 30 percent larger than Earth with a 14.4-day orbit

revisions.change: Record drafted from the cited sources.

Corrected the summary, which said that the AJ published the paper in December 2017 when it was only accepted and posted to arXiv then and published on 30 January 2018, widened the 96 percent figure to cover false positives as NASA states, reworded the eight-planet claim to the first exoplanetary system with eight planets, and noted that validation used follow-up data already on the Kepler Community Follow-up Program rather than no new observations.

claim_basis: One independent press release, the makers' peer-reviewed study and the makers' preprint are on file. There is no independent study or report and no finding by a regulator or court.
